extracted_by: hand, T-0261 — the Chicago American read, June to August 1835
note: Volume I, Number 4, and the densest local column of the run: page 3 column 5 carries twenty advertisements in fifty lines. New to the corpus here — a livery partnership dissolving, an auction room on South Water Street west of J. Wright's holding its first sale ON THE SCENE DATE, a vacant corner lot named by lot and block, a wholesale wine and liquor store in Dearborn Street, a tailoring shop, School District No. 2's Meeting House, and Philo Carpenter's drug store. Page 3 column 6 puts the American's own office on the record a second time, as a place subscriptions are taken.

claims.normalized: [From the Sangamon Jou[rnal]. STATE BANK OF ILLINO[IS]. The following is a list of th[e officers] of the State Bank of Illinois a[nd its] Branches. The Directors [have deter]mined to establish branches [at … ] and Chicago, but the officers [of those in]stitutions have not been made [known … the a]mount of stock subscribed was [… mil]lion[ and s]even thousand [five] hundr[ed …] We learn that the bank has [taken] the brick building on the squa[re, near] the court house, which will be [fitted up for] banking hours, and that [it will go] into operation within [th]ree or [four … ] STATE BANK. Thomas Mather, President.
claims.notes: NO BANK IN CHICAGO AT THE SCENE DATE, and this is the notice that says so. The State Bank of Illinois has DETERMINED to establish a branch at Chicago and 'the officers of those institutions have not been made known' — so five days before 1835-07-01 the branch exists as a decision and not as a building, an officer or a counter. READ THE DATELINE BEFORE READING THE BUILDING. This paragraph is reprinted 'From the Sangamon Jou[rnal]', and the brick building on the square near the court house that the bank has taken is SPRINGFIELD'S square and SPRINGFIELD'S court house, not Chicago's. Chicago in June 1835 has neither a brick bank nor a court house — the Circuit Court sits here (1835-08-22) and the county court-house is not built until the autumn. The trap is worth writing down because a search of this corpus for 'the square' and 'the court house' finds this sentence first, and a reader in a hurry would put a brick bank on the Public Square. It is also why the letter-list sweep across the American's thirteen issues returned exactly one hit for 'list of' and it was this: a list of bank officers, in another town.

claims.notes: A HOUSE ON LAKE STREET, TO LET, in the week before the scene date — and a legal land description beside it that this project can actually resolve. Township 37 North, Range 19 [East], third principal meridian is the survey the town itself sits in, so the forty acres are county land within a few miles of the plat. THE RANGE'S DIRECTION IS THE PROBLEM: the transcription reads 'want of ube third principal', which is 'west of the third principal meridian', and Range 19 WEST of the third principal meridian is nowhere near Chicago while Range 19 EAST is Lake Township. The reading is quoted as printed and the discrepancy is recorded rather than corrected — a single-pass OCR 'want'/'east' confusion is likely and unproven, and this project does not silently move forty acres across a state.

claims.notes: A LIVERY BUSINESS IN CHICAGO IN JUNE 1835 — the first this corpus has, and the trade implies a stable and a yard the town model has no documented instance of. It is recorded through its DISSOLUTION, so `contradicts` is set and the partnership does not stand at the scene date; what the notice documents positively is that the trade was being carried on here until 1835-06-15. THE SECOND PARTNER IS A SINGLE LETTER, 'J', and is not identified. Note the shape of the evidence: two of the run's four business dissolutions (this and Goss & Cobb) are the only reason those trades are documented at all, because neither firm's own advertisement survives in the American.

claims.notes: A SOUTH WATER STREET AUCTION ROOM OPENING IN THE WEEK OF THE SCENE DATE, and the placement is the good kind: a named neighbour, J. Wright's, with the new room WEST of it, on a street corner the same sentence half-names. THE SALE DATE IS AMBIGUOUS AND IS NOT RESOLVED: 'Hid first Public Sale will take place' runs into 'duy the lat day of July' across the line break, which is either 'the 1st day of July' — the scene date itself — or 'the last day of July', and the same phrase repeats in the next sentence with the same ambiguity. Both readings are consistent with the characters and this project does not need it to be the scene date badly enough to decide it. THE PROPRIETOR is cut after 'W. MONT' and no person is minted. The quoted line carries the segmenter's coordinate telemetry inside the advertisement, which is why it stands in the verbatim quote.

claims.notes: THE PAINT SHELF OF A CHICAGO STORE IN JUNE 1835, listed pigment by pigment: white lead, red lead, Spanish brown, Venetian red, spruce yellow, yellow ochre, rose pink, gold and silver leaf, and six oils. That is a directly usable material list — this project paints buildings and has been reasoning about their colour from period practice in general rather than from what was for sale in this town in this month. TWO ADVERTISEMENTS ARE QUOTED TOGETHER and the reason is the segmenter: the pot-ash notice signed by Hubbard & Co. begins in the middle of line 372, inside the paint list's last line, and the paint list's own signature is destroyed there. THE PAINTS ARE NOT HUBBARD'S. This claim first attributed them to Hubbard & Co., on the only signature the passage carries, and reading forward one week refuted it: the identical list runs on 1835-07-04 page 3 column 6 lines 339-341 signed 'PHILO CARPENTER, Chicago, June 27, 1835' — the same copy date as this printing, which is what identifies the two as one advertisement. The goods are therefore recorded on Carpenter's business, and only the pot-ash notice beginning inside line 372 belongs to Hubbard & Co. The wrong reading is left recorded here rather than quietly swapped, because it is the exact shape of mistake this column invites.

claims.notes: A SECOND DRUGGIST, FULLY NAMED: Philo Carpenter, selling wholesale to other druggists and merchants. So the town supports two drug stores three weeks before the scene date, one of them supplying the trade. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SETTLE ABOUT 'CARPENTER'. 1835-06-13 signs a leather stock 'CABPRNTYS' and 1835-06-20 signs a window-glass consignment 'CARPEN', both cut, and neither was minted as a person. This claim does NOT merge them into Philo Carpenter: a druggist selling harness leather and crown glass is possible in a frontier town and is not documented, and the surname alone is not identity — the same rule that keeps 'Cohen, P.' and 'Cohen, J.' apart. Those two businesses stay under their own names in the gazetteer and this note is where the question is recorded. NO ADDRESS is printed.
